newsitem.title: USA: Richardson will try to arrange Zaire peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Richardson will try to arrange Zaire peace talks.

text.p: American diplomat Bill Richardson will go to Zaire soon to try to arrange peace talks between Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila, the White House said on Saturday.

Richardson, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations and a frequent diplomatic troubleshooter for President Bill Clinton, plans to meet both Mobutu and Kabila "to urge them to find a peaceful resolution to the current conflict," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said in a statement.
"He will press both sides to agree to halt the fighting and launch serious negotiations to form an inclusive transitional government leading to free and fair democratic elections," McCurry said.
It was not clear when Richardson would leave, but an official said it would not be this weekend.
Kabila's rebel forces, known as the Alliance of Democratic Froces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire, have seized more than half of Zaire since October.

The United States has signalled that Mobutu, once treated as a strategic ally and a Cold War bulwark against communism in Africa, should step down and clear the way for a transitional government in Zaire. But Mobutu has refused.
A White House official said Richardson's mission was not to pressure Mobutu to resign and go into exile.
"He's going to try to get Mobutu and Kabila to talk," the official said.

Richardson, while a member of the House of Representatives, carried out sensitive missions for Clinton in Burma, Haiti and Iraq. He went to North Korea last November to nail down a nuclear agreement and win the release of a young American detained for three months on espionage charges.

The United States, Britain and France, among other nations, have been under pressure from U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan and his envoy, Mohammed Sahnoun, to use their influence to coax Kabila and Mobutu to the negotiating table.
Sahnoun was reported by U.N. sources to be hopeful that talks could take place and wanted the United States to intervene in getting direct negotiations started.

Libreville, the capitol of Gabon, is the current frontrunner for such talks, although Brazzaville, Congo and Luanda, Rwanda are also being considered so that Mobutu, suffering from cancer, would not have to travel far.
McCurry said Richardson during his mission would also underscore America's deep concern on the humanitarian situation, refugee repatriation and human rights in Zaire.
Kabila has faced a worldwide outcry after his forces in eastern Zaire refused to allow U.N. humanitarian groups to bring food to tens of thousands of Rwandan refugees caught amid Zaire's civil war.
Kabila travelled to Kisangani in northeastern Zaire on Saturday for talks on the fate of nearly 100,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees missing in the jungle.
